submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the digits of a numeral that is the bound of a comparison: the second number of a range ('between 15 and 20 percent', 'aged 18 to 65', '20 to 30 students') or an age/threshold value in a statement about people ('aged 65', 'older than 55', 'under 15', 'a quarter of the population is over 65'), where it reaches roughly 2-30x the scan's scale. Numerals used as plain values or labels ('in 1999', 'costs 40 dollars', 'page 65', 'about 65 million', '65 percent of the population') and comparators applied to a single object's physical dimension ('the wall is 65 metres', 'the temperature is over 30 degrees') leave it near zero, and a numeral-free sentence gives only a weak few-tenths background (0.2-0.5, near the record's active line) rather than true silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The city council released its long-awaited flood resilience strategy on Tuesday, a two-hundred-page document that sets out how the waterfront district will be protected over the next three decades. The plan follows eighteen months of consultation with engineers, insurers, residents' groups and the regional water authority, and it replaces the piecemeal approach that has governed the district since the seawall was last rebuilt.

The strategy divides the waterfront into four zones. In the northern zone, where the ground sits barely a metre above mean high water, the council proposes a combination of raised embankments, permeable paving and a chain of small retention ponds that will fill during heavy rain and drain slowly afterwards. The central zone, which contains most of the district's shops and restaurants, will be protected by a removable barrier system that can be deployed within six hours of a severe weather warning. The southern zone, dominated by warehouses and a container terminal, will rely mainly on improved drainage and a revised emergency plan agreed with port operators. Engineers stress that the zones are not sealed off from one another; a failure in one would quickly affect its neighbours, which is why the works are sequenced rather than scattered.

Funding remains the most contentious element. Officers estimate the full programme will cost roughly 1.1 billion dollars over thirty years, though they concede that the figure could rise if sea levels track the upper end of the official projections. A separate maintenance budget of about 12 million dollars a year has been pencilled in, though critics note that maintenance has historically been the first item cut when revenues fall short. The mayor has promised that no borrowing will be required before the next municipal bond issue.

The section that has attracted most attention concerns relocation. The review board expects between 300 and 400 households to be moved before the main works begin, most of them from streets closest to the old quay. Residents will be offered alternative accommodation within the district wherever possible, and the council has promised that nobody will be asked to leave before a replacement home is ready. Tenants' associations have welcomed the principle but want the guarantees written into the plan rather than left to officers' discretion.

Opposition councillors have focused on the timetable, arguing that the first embankment works will not start until the 2029 financial year at the earliest, leaving low-lying streets exposed through several more storm seasons. The mayor's office counters that the design work cannot be rushed and that interim measures, including temporary pumps and a revised warning system, will be in place well before then.

The plan will go to a full council vote next month and, if approved, to the regional authority for final sign-off. Public submissions close in six weeks, and several community groups have already announced that they will seek changes to the relocation provisions and to the proposed boundary of the northern zone. Officers have said that a revised version of the document will be published in the spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long report whose only comparison bound ('between 300 and 400 households') sits deep in the passage, testing that the claimed feature still fires in long context.
